title: Half a Wave
blurb: Someone keeps chalking drills on Wren's bench, and in the Ropewalk Drum Wren must trust a partner's timing to the instant.

blocks.text: Chalk squeaks across wood, downstairs, in the dark.
By the time I'm down the stair the workshop is empty and the street door is swinging on its latch. I didn't stop for boots. On my banker, in big square capitals, the chalk dust still loose:
"Boots off," I read aloud. "Feel the Raise, not the note."
No name.
I told the side I felt Gorm's pitch through my feet, and Dov laughed. There's one man in Caddrow who wouldn't laugh. He's deaf, and he swears he'll never set foot in a Drum again.
So either he lied, or somebody else was listening.
All right. I know whose hand it is.

The capitals belong to a man who learned his letters late and big. The chalk is the soft yellow stick the Lime Barrow uses to write up the price of ale. Two nights ago that man stood on the last step of the Kilnyard stair, one boot hanging over the floor like it was cold water, and asked who taught me to stand like that.
"A dead man," I told him, "and a lot of stone."
He watched my mouth a long time after I'd finished. Then he went back up the stair, and his boots never touched the Drum.
So I pretend I don't know. It's kinder to both of us.
I'm already barefoot, so I do what the banker says. The workshop flags are cold enough to make my teeth hurt. I put a palm on the banker's stone top and shut my eyes.

A cart turns into the street. I feel the iron tyre on the cobbles before I hear it, a grinding in the balls of my feet that climbs my shins. The baker two doors down drops his shutter. Then my own heart, which I could do without.

Feel the Raise, not the note. The Raise is the warning. The note is the thing that hurts you. In Round One, Gorm's hum came up through my boot soles like a cart a street away. Bare, it's a cart in the room.
Next morning there's another one.
PALM ON THE STONE. HUM LOW. HUM HIGH. LEARN WHICH IS WHICH WITH YOUR EYES SHUT.
I do it with my eyes shut until the baker knocks to ask if I'm ill.
The morning after, I leave one of my own, under his: COME TO ROPEWALK. ROUND TWO.
The morning after that, under mine, underlined twice: NO DRUMS.
Fair enough. Banker's grief, but fair enough.
The last one is there the morning of the match, and it isn't words. Two stick figures on two squares. A gap between them. A wavy line drawn across the gap. Underneath:
HALF A WAVE. ONE INSTANT. NOT TWO.
I know that picture. It's cut over the door of the Kilnyard Drum, older than anybody. Sef says he has it. Somebody had it first.
I don't wipe the banker. I don't much like lintels these days, but I like being told things.
Ropewalk is away. Away means no gate. The tin stays at three crowns.

The Ropewalk is a shed a quarter-mile long where they twist hemp into rope, and the Drum is under the far end of it, down a ramp that smells of tar. The facing is a year or two old. Tight joints, clean beds, somebody's good honest work. I approve of it as a mason and resent it as a visitor.
I sit on the bottom of the ramp and unlace.
Dov stops dead. "What are you doing."
"Taking my boots off."
"In public. Wren. There's a gallery. There are people up there who've seen me play."
"Then they've seen worse."
He puts a hand over his eyes. "That's not a stance. That's a confession."
"Three things," says Sef, not looking up from his notebook. "One, there's no rule. Two, it's cold. Three." He looks at my feet. "Interesting."
"Wren Halloway," says Oduya, very quietly, "you will have chilblains by the Half, and you will not come to me for goose fat."
Marten just says, "Aye, well," and watches my mouth.

The floor is gritty with bloom and so cold it bites. Under the cold it's talking. The gallery's feet. Someone dragging a crate on the ramp. A Caller somewhere humming scales to warm up, every note arriving in my soles a heartbeat ahead of my one good ear.
The Warden swings his tell-weight. "Pace five." Sef registers Marten and me as Dampers.
Across the Drum, Ropewalk's Callers come out together, red-haired, the same face twice, hair tied back with rope-yarn.

"The Teague twins," says Sef. "Pinch and Twist. Pinch sings high, Twist sings low, and they have never started a sentence separately in their lives. Four things. One, they throw chords. Two voices in one beam. Two, they don't miss much. Three, I don't know yet. Four, stay on your stands."
Their first throw, the twins draw in a breath together, both shoulders up at once, and a count later Pinch lifts her hand.
The Raise comes up through my feet in two pieces. One high and thin, like a wire. One low and wide, like a cellar door. Two lead-ins, two pitches, one beam aimed at our Last Plate.

I know which one matters before the voicing. The high one sits right on our pitch peg. The low one is nowhere near it, because in the Breath before, Oduya walked our plate up a semitone, somewhere Twist's cellar-door voice can't climb.
"A plate is a stockpot," Oduya told me on the cart, "not a kettle. You don't keep it where they like it. You keep it where they don't."

The chord crawls across the Drum, a faint glow at its front, slow as a man crossing a room. Marten and I stand in it. The low note shoves through us and strikes our plate two semitones off and rattles like a tin tray. Nothing. The high one shoves through us too, and loses a weight for each of us, and arrives too light to ring.
Second chord, the same. Third, Dov Peals, the Lamplighter, and tells the whole gallery its name.
But I'm standing there with two pitches going through my body, and I'm doing sums.

The note on the lintel is half a wave apart. Fine. That's one gap for one length. These are two lengths. One gap can't be half of two different lengths. Any apprentice with a rule could tell you that.
So whatever the lintel is, it kills one pitch. The other one we Quell, or we let it strike. There is no third thing.
Then Pinch throws a four.
It goes through Marten, through me. Four becomes two. Two on our peg is still a Peal. Three counts of our own plate singing at us. One all.
"Aye, well," says Marten.
On the ninth, Twist strains up into a note that nearly cracks, and Oduya's peg can't run that far in one Breath. That one rings too. One to two.
Nobody draws. Sef doesn't call it, and Marten never draws. I'm not drawing a four to save one Peal when there's a whole Half to come and a whole bond behind it.
At the Half, the Long Ground hums us all down to nothing, and my toes have gone the colour of slate.
Sef has stopped writing. He's watching the twins across the floor, and for a while all he says is, "Interesting."
Then: "Three things. One, no. Two things. One. They breathe together, a count before every chord. In, then the Raise. Every time."
"We know," says Dov. "They're twins. It's charming."
"Two. They do it on our throws as well. They breathe in together, and then they step to block you. They read your Raise and get their bodies in your line before it ends."
"I'm aware they're in my line, Sef. I've been throwing through them all night."

"On the in-breath," Sef says, "their feet are set. They're getting ready to Raise, even when it isn't their turn. They can't move on it. So you wait." He holds up a hand. "You wait in the Breath until their shoulders come up. Then you Raise. By the time they breathe out, your Raise has ended, and if they step, that's hush-stepping."
Dov stares at him. "You want me to time my throws to their breathing. I'm a Caller, not a midwife."
"I want you to win."
Dov considers this from several angles. "Fine," he says. "But I'm naming it."

He waits. The Breath runs out. Both red heads lift, both pairs of shoulders rise, and Dov's hand goes up. The twins twitch and stay planted, because the alternative is a penalty Peal. His note goes past them like a cart through an open gate. Their Damper draws it and staggers.
The next one he calls the Bowline. It Peals. Two all.
Three throws later, on their in-breath again, he Peals again. Three to two. Dov bows to the gallery, which boos him, which he likes better.

Their chords keep coming. Oduya keeps walking our peg. Low notes rattle. High notes come through Marten and me and arrive too light, or a hair off, and die on the brass. The twins are going hoarse. They're saving something.
Last throw of the match. Theirs. Three to two.
In the Breath, Oduya walks our plate up again. Pinch looks at the peg. Then at her brother. Then at me.
If the high note Peals, it's three all and Sudden Peal. If it's hard and true and Peals for six counts, it's three points, and we lose five to three in a Drum that smells of tar.
They breathe in. Pinch's hand goes up.

The Raise comes up through my soles. The high lead-in is clean and dead on our peg. The low one is nowhere near. So it's the high one. At pace five, that pitch is three paces long. Half of it is a pace and a half.

Marten's on the stand ahead of me along the line of the beam. Sef walked the Ropewalk floor chart into us on the cart. Those two stands are a pace and a half apart, near enough that my feet can't tell the difference.
It's the lintel. We're standing in it.
"Stay," I tell Marten, before the Raise ends. He stays.
The twins voice. The chord comes off them with weight in it, a four at least. The front glows and starts to crawl. Four counts to cross. A slow walk across a room.
"On my now," I say. "Not near it. On it. One instant."
Marten watches my mouth. "Aye, well."

I can't Quell this one alone. That's two Marks and four ring, and I'm thinking about my hands on a chisel handle. I can't body-block it either: four through two of us is still a Peal. There's only the picture on the lintel.
Three counts. Two. The low note and the high note come up through the floor into my heels, the wire and the cellar door.
"Now."
And I hold back.

Only a hair. Just long enough to feel him go. I don't decide to. My body decides, the way you check a block's bed with your palm before you trust your weight to it. I've never stood half a wave from anyone. I want to feel his draw land first.
I feel it land. A thump in the stone between my feet, like a mallet on the far end of a beam.
Then I draw, and there's nothing left to draw.

Marten takes the whole high note alone. Weight four. It goes into him and he rocks on his stand and his hands curl up at his sides like dead leaves. The low note goes past us both, strikes our Last Plate a long way off its peg and rattles. A tin tray. Nothing.
The Warden's weight stops swinging.
Three to two. Kilnyard hold.

The gallery is making a noise in my good ear. Dov is shouting something with his own name in it. Oduya's hand is on my shoulder and she is saying "Wren Halloway" in the voice that means trouble later.
I'm looking at Marten.

He's never drawn. Not once, all season, and the side reads it as an old Damper's caution and doesn't say a word. Tonight he drew because I told him to, on my count, on the instant I named. Then I gave him two instants instead of one and left him alone in a hard note.
Half a wave. One instant. Not two. It was written on my banker in chalk.
The Warden crosses to Marten's stand and sets the foot of his listening rod on the stone. Holds it. Lifts it.
"Thirty-six, Sallow," he says, loud, for the sheet. "Four left."
Marten nods.
He nods late. Not when the words reach us. When the Warden's mouth stops moving.

Sef is beside me. He isn't looking at the Warden, the way every Scribe in the Cellar Ring looks at the Warden when a number's called. He's looking at his own Damper's face. I watch his eyes go from Marten's eyes to the Warden's lips, and back, and his pencil stops on the page.
Marten took the note I didn't trust him with, and Sef has just seen that Marten can't hear his own number.
